brief.head: Where FDI begins
brief.text: A foreign stake of 10 per cent or more counts as FDI under the OECD and IMF definition, Ajay Shah said. At 9 per cent, it does not. {111-C01}

brief.head: Coffee in Vienna
brief.text: FDI by India is a separate flow from FDI in India. Shah’s example: Cafe Coffee Day in Vienna, of which he has a photograph. {111-J13}

brief.head: Dodging the border
brief.text: Put up trade barriers and foreigners build minimal plants behind them, assembling semi-knocked-down cars. Jagdish Bhagwati called it tariff-jumping FDI: arbitrage around policy, Shah said. {111-C09}

brief.head: A ladder upside down
brief.text: Normally the best firms invest abroad. In Indian software, Shah’s research found, firms that body-shop staff into the UK and Germany are weaker than those exporting from home. {111-C12}

brief.head: An exporting show
brief.text: With 30 per cent of its audience overseas, Shah declared this show an exporter. Varma, fearing an income-tax raid, said: “My head is spinning, bro.” {111-J08}

thought.text: Then we should view FDI as the crucible where the knowledge is made.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that workers who learn in foreign firms are FDI’s real prize

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on why India should love foreign investment
lead.head: A love letter to foreign capital
body: Amit Varma promised his gentle readers an episode not about money but about love. Ajay Shah, he said, had confided that he has five great loves. {111-J01}
Shah named firm productivity, capital account openness and inflation targeting. The fifth, and the subject of the hour, was foreign direct investment.

Their first meeting came in the early 1980s, when an American from Corning Glass visited Shah’s father, hoping to build a glass factory in India. The father told him the Indian state would not allow it.
Shah called the subject “a critical battlefront” for the next 25 years of the Indian story, and no been-there, done-that topic.
## An honest escape valve

The heart of his case was a dream. A country admits that its institutions are bad, and walls off a patch of land, say one square kilometre, where foreign factories are spared local labour law, tax harassment, visa trouble and customs duties.
“It takes enormous honesty to say this openly,” Shah said.
The state gives up its depredations. In exchange, thousands of workers get jobs, and the state collects income tax on their wages and GST on their spending.
That, he argued, was the greatness of the Chinese model under Deng Xiaoping: FDI into China ran under good institutions, because the state was able to back off. {111-C03}
The bigger prize is knowledge. Workers in foreign firms learn the global frontier of productivity, then move to other jobs or start firms of their own, taking it with them.

India, Shah said, never said these paragraphs to itself clearly. Talk of a level playing field misses the point. The bargain only works if foreign firms escape what Indian regulators, capital controls and visa rules do to everyone else. {111-C05}
“If there is a magic in FDI, it is Deng Xiaoping,” he said.

Varma stressed that this is no argument against fixing India’s institutions, a fight that will go on. Meanwhile, “little islands of freedom” are worth having: “let’s not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.”
## The money that can leave
Indian policy circles treat FDI as the good guy and portfolio investment as hot money. Shah said that view comes “from a place of deep insecurity”, and is analytically wrong.
Foreigners already know India’s weaknesses and price them in, he said, and India has never had a big crisis from foreign portfolio exit.
Contrary to many Indian economists, he argued, portfolio investment needs better institutions than FDI does: trustworthy accounts, audits, a stock market and a depository. {111-C07}
The resistance is political. Portfolio money gives Indian business more buyers for its shares and a lower cost of capital; FDI gives it competition. Shah credited that insight to Ila Patnaik.
## A rare window
Shah closed on hope. The breakdown of the China model and America’s turmoil over tariffs have reshaped the world economy. The surge is not yet in the data, he admitted, but the conditions are right.
“I think 2025 is an important moment in India’s history,” he said. {111-C13}
Varma had the last word. “And if it doesn’t happen, we are playing a long game.”

second.label: Investment treaties
second.head: Insured by a slap
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why India should compensate the investors it expropriates
body: Foreign investors need a predictable environment, Amit Varma said, not the “retrospective taxation kind of nonsense” done to Vodafone. {#vodafone} Ajay Shah’s answer is the bilateral investment treaty, in which India promises to compensate foreign investors whenever any level of the Indian state expropriates them.

Paying out $1 billion a year to stabilise $100 billion of FDI is a good deal, Shah said, like an insurance premium. {#insurance} And a slap in the face each time the state misbehaves is how checks and balances get built. {111-C10}

But officials who lost cases took them personally, and a machismo set in. A new model treaty in 2016 abandoned many good ideas. {#modelbit} Today, Shah said, India is increasingly hostile to such treaties.

quote.text: It’s actually brilliantly incentive compatible for the Indian state to pay money when the Indian state misbehaves.

second.caption: investment treaties as insurance

third.head: Too proud to stoop
body: India’s distrust of foreign capital runs deep, Ajay Shah said. “There is a deep anti-foreigner streak in India. There is a deep anti-Western streak in India.” In deep ways, he added, it has fed into Indian failure. {111-C11}
There is also a cult of third-worldism, in which multinationals became a bad word. In its old picture, he said, poor helpless Bengali workers are exploited in a Texas Instruments factory. {#texas}

A newer arrogance has joined it: India is so important that foreign companies have no choice but to come, so why stoop? Development goes well, Shah said, when policymakers honestly pursue growth, and badly when pride creeps in.
Amit Varma blamed a toxic, insular nationalism of the we-don’t-need-the-world kind. “All trade, all human connection is positive sum,” he said.
third.caption: India’s anti-foreigner streak

p2.title: Foreign affairs
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s argument for foreign direct investment, chapter by chapter, with Amit Varma asking the questions

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Ten per cent, seven numbers
sections.caption: what counts as FDI
body: Loosely, we think of FDI as a foreigner building a factory in India. Ajay Shah’s definition is tighter: a foreigner holding a substantial, long-term stake in an Indian production arrangement. Buy shares in an Indian bakery company such as Britannia and sell them next week, and that is portfolio investment.
Where is the line? The OECD and the IMF have agreed on a minimum equity holding of 10 per cent. At 9 per cent, it is not FDI. {111-C01}

Other things count too. A foreign parent’s loan to its Indian subsidiary is FDI. So is a foreign private equity fund’s 11 per cent stake in a completely Indian company, though that bothers some people. Profits a foreign-owned operation reinvests in India, rather than repatriating, are booked as a brand new FDI flow that year.
## A menu for propagandists

The balance of payments gives “beautiful, trusted, high quality” data, Shah said. But there are seven numbers: gross inflow, repatriation and net for FDI in India, the matching three for FDI by India, and a “net net” overall. {#seven}

Propagandists of every stripe pick whichever flatters their story. Shah’s surest sign of propaganda is a chart titled simply “FDI”. Proper labelling, he complained, is missing “fifty per cent of the time, seventy per cent of the time”. {111-C02}
~ Amit Varma was suitably chastened. “I’m never gonna say FDI in front of you again,” he said. {111-J03}

quote.text: If you say FDI, you’re a propagandist. Okay, you have to be precise.

sections.label: The dream
sections.head: One square kilometre of sanity
sections.caption: the dream of FDI
body: Picture a country with bad institutions, Ajay Shah said, that gets itself together just enough to say: for this one square kilometre, build your factory and you will be protected from the depredations of the local institutions. {#squarekm}

No local labour law, no messing with taxation, no visa trouble, no customs duties on goods coming in or going out. The cleanest form is a bonded warehouse, where imports arrive fully exempt and finished goods leave for the world. {#bonded}
The state gives up its depredations. In return, thousands of workers get jobs, and it collects income tax on their wages and GST on their spending.
## Deng’s bargain

This was the greatness of the Chinese and South East Asian model. Deng Xiaoping’s China accepted that fixing its Companies Act and GST would take a hundred years, and would not hold its breath. {#hundredyears}
The second prize is knowledge. People in foreign firms learn the global frontier of productivity, then leave to work for other companies or start their own. {111-C04}
~ India, Shah said, never said these paragraphs to itself clearly enough, and that is why FDI here has never quite worked out well.

quote.text: FDI into China operates under good institutions because the Chinese state is able to back off.

sections.label: The other money
sections.head: Hot money, cool heads
sections.caption: portfolio investment
body: In Indian policy circles, FDI is the good guy and portfolio investment is hot money that can buy today and sell tomorrow. Ajay Shah traced the fear to insecurity: a portfolio investor can sell and leave, and that frightens an insecure Indian. {111-C06}
His advice came from love: “If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn’t, it never was.” {111-J05}

The fear is also analytically wrong, he said. Foreigners already know India’s weaknesses, and those are priced in. Foreign investors are no monolith: every day brings large gross buying and selling and a tiny net. And when shocks like the COVID lockdown come, Indians and foreigners sell alike. {#covid}
## Paper you can trust

In fact, Shah argued, portfolio investment needs better institutions than FDI does. {111-C07} A factory needs only a state that backs off and “three pages of rules”. An investor in Tokyo, handed a piece of paper saying he owns a thousand shares of Reliance, needs trustworthy accounts, audit, a stock market and a depository.
That is why China never got portfolio investment going, Shah said, while India, with a hundred and fifty years of accounting tradition, can. {#accounting}
~ Who, he asked, is any economist to call one flow good and another bad? Private people should decide; the government’s job is to build institutions.

quote.text: It is FDI that demands a lower institutional quality and FPI demands a higher institutional quality.

sections.label: Who wants what
sections.head: Buyers welcome, rivals not
sections.caption: the politics of foreign money
body: If the economics is so clear, Amit Varma asked, why does the consensus run the other way? Ajay Shah’s answer turned on who gains.

A foreigner with a factory in India will want to sell in India too. A foreigner making cars hurts Premier Padmini; Indian retail is angry at Amazon and Walmart. For the Indian rich, FDI means competition. {111-C08}

Portfolio money is the opposite: more buyers for their shares and bonds, and a lower cost of capital. Shah credited the insight to Ila Patnaik. Varma summed it up: “On one side of the debate you have securities. On the other side you have insecurities.” {111-J06}

A pure export enclave, Shah thought, would be politically harmless; it has failed for want of intellectual clarity. India has an SEZ Act of 2005, but never immunised foreign firms from Indian institutions. {#sez2005}
## Behind the tariff wall

Trade barriers bring a distortion of their own. In the early 1990s, Jagdish Bhagwati called it tariff-jumping FDI: foreigners doing minimal assembly of semi-knocked-down cars to sell behind the wall. Much of India’s car industry, Shah said, is like that. {111-C09}
~ Barriers raise the cost of inputs too. Imported raw materials for artificial fabric carry 10 per cent duties, Shah said, which make Indian yarn, cloth and shirts less competitive. {#tenpercent}

quote.text: So for the Indian rich, FDI is not interesting. FDI is not attractive because it is competition for their own businesses.

sections.label: Keeping faith
sections.head: Humble pie for the state
sections.caption: protecting foreign investors
body: Amit Varma recalled that when he first heard of SEZs, his “purest libertarian mind” asked why the whole country should not be one, and reached for a line of verse: “Into that heaven of freedom, my father, let my country awake.” {111-J07}
His questions were practical. How do you protect foreigners from a state he called “fundamentally a parasite for its own people”? And how do you give them predictability?

China managed it, Ajay Shah said, with a trusted, predictable mechanism, until Xi Jinping: with a populist regime, all bets are off. Elsewhere, the answer is the bilateral investment treaty, under which India compensates foreign investors it expropriates.
## Team India

The union government signs, so it must pay even when a state or city government misbehaved. “We are team India,” Shah said. But frontline officials detested payouts, and took lost cases personally, as bad for careers and budgets.
Shah wants humility: accept a slap in the face each time the state fumbles, diagnose what went wrong and fix it. {#slapped}
Instead, he said, the state turned arrogant: “It’s my sovereign right to expropriate you. How dare you tell me that I have to pay money.” {#sovereign}
~ Varma had a word for domestic firms. A level playing field matters, he said, and he would fight for it. “But don’t deny this to foreign firms.”

quote.text: The Indian state should get slapped in the face when the Indian state misbehaves.

sections.label: Graduation day
sections.head: Raju becomes a multinational
sections.caption: Indian firms going global
body: Amit Varma borrowed the chapter’s title from Aziz Mirza’s film *Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman*. He just likes the title, he said: Raju wants to be a gentleman, and Indian firms want to be global firms. {111-J10}
Ajay Shah’s hope for India rests on its elite. The top end of the country’s knowledge spectrum, he said, is “just out of the world”. {#elite}

The old third-worldism saw a developing country only as the helpless recipient of FDI. But in the last twenty years, Shah said, Indian firms have become multinationals on a beautiful scale, something unimaginable when he was young. He, Dilek Demirbas and Ila Patnaik wrote the first paper on it, *Graduating to Globalisation*.
## Up the ladder

The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model ranks firms by productivity: the weakest stay domestic, better ones export, the best do FDI abroad. Hundreds of Indian firms, Shah said, are now multinationals. {#hundreds}

Indian software turns the ladder upside down. Firms that sit in India while foreign business comes to them are the most productive; the body shoppers who carry their people into the UK and Germany are weaker. {111-C12}
~ By that test, Shah said, this show has graduated too: 30 per cent of its audience is overseas. {#audience}

quote.text: It’s upside down that FDI Indian software companies are worse than exporting Indian software companies.

side.boxText: Deng Xiaoping, Ajay Shah said, saw that fixing China’s Companies Act and GST would take a hundred years. So he built a trusted, predictable interface for foreigners in the meantime. His dream, Shah joked, was that there would be no Xi Jinping. {111-J02}

contQuote.text: The magic of FDI is not in having foreign companies stand in line and be treated by Indian regulators and Indian capital controls and Indian passport visa problems, just like anybody else. Then what’s the point?

stories.end: And sure enough, they've got a great collapse of FDI into
stories.caption: Fernandes, Deng and Xi
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how India and China drove investors away
stories.head: From Fernandes to Xi, a rerun
body: Ajay Shah’s simplest picture of FDI is a foreigner building a factory in India, and its simplest opposite is George Fernandes. Fernandes, he said, drove IBM and Coca-Cola out of India. {#fernandes1}
IBM had operated in India, supporting the IBM mainframes used here. Fernandes created conditions under which it chose to pack its bags and leave. The same happened to Coca-Cola.
The conditions, as Shah described them, were the kind investors dread: you will do technology transfer into India, you will do an IPO in India, you will have a joint venture in India.

China, for a while, went the other way. Deng Xiaoping accepted that its institutions were bad, and that fixing them would take a hundred years. Meanwhile he built a predictable interface where the state left foreigners alone. “Deng Xiaoping’s dream was there will be no Xi Jinping,” Shah said. {111-J02}
Then came Xi Jinping. Rules on technology transfer and joint ventures crept back, Shah said: the same kind of conditions Fernandes had imposed in India. {111-S04}

“So this is the loss of clarity,” he said. There had been too much kindness in the way people spoke about FDI, and not enough intellectual clarity. The very reason the FDI-led model is so good, he said, is that it overcomes the failure of domestic institutions. Sure enough, FDI into China collapsed.
~ For how China came to this, Shah pointed listeners to the hosts’ earlier episode *The China Model is Broken*. {111-R04}
stories.why: A country’s welcome to foreign capital is not a permanent feature. China’s, Shah suggested, rested on a political commitment to leave foreigners alone, and the FDI went when the commitment did. {111-C03}

stories.caption: the man from Corning Glass
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s first brush with foreign investment
stories.head: Glass ceiling, made in India
body: In the early 1980s, Ajay Shah happened to be around when an American from Corning Glass came to meet his father. Shah dates the visit by his father’s death in 1984.
Corning wanted to set up a factory in India to make glass. It was a nice idea, Shah’s father agreed: there would be demand for such glass, for television picture tubes and so on.

But this is banned and that is banned, he told his guest, and the Indian state would ban it. The American was baffled that a government would want to stop a company building factories in its country. {111-S01}
~ That was Shah’s first brush with FDI. Amit Varma reframed it on the spot. “What you love is freedom, isn’t it, Ajay?” he asked. {#freedom}

quote.text: And this guy was very baffled, why would the government want to prevent us from building factories in India.

stories.start: So I want to give you an example that Nokia built a facility
stories.end: Those have to be kept out when you're doing FDI.
stories.caption: Nokia’s exit from Tamil Nadu
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a marquee investor that walked out
stories.head: Welcome mat, then the taxman
body: Nokia did exactly what India says it wants from foreign companies. It built a manufacturing facility in Tamil Nadu.
Then, Ajay Shah said, “the Indian state went after them with income tax and freezing of assets and so on. And in the end, Nokia packed up and left.” {111-S02}

For Shah, the failure was one of intellectual clarity. India lacked the discipline to wall off the normal depredations the state inflicts on Indian companies. Those, he said, “have to be kept out when you’re doing FDI”.

~ Otherwise there is nothing special about FDI. Indian entrepreneurs are equally good and can buy foreign technology, and the country faces a 200-year journey to becoming an advanced economy. {#twohundred}
stories.why: Inviting foreign investors is the easy half. Unless the state walls them off from the treatment it metes out to Indian firms, Shah argued, even a marquee investment can walk out. {111-C05}

stories.start: Again and again through world history, we have seen that knowledge diffusion happening.
stories.end: stepped out and started their own businesses, and so on, the whole thing went.
stories.caption: Bangladesh’s garment trade
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how knowledge leaves the factory gate
stories.head: Sewing the seeds in Bangladesh
body: Bangladesh’s garment industry, in Ajay Shah’s telling, did not begin with Bangladeshi firms. Taiwanese and South Korean companies came first and started garment businesses there. {111-S03}
Local people went to work for them and learned the trade. Then they stepped out and started garment businesses of their own, and the industry spread from there.

For Shah this is the ultimate prize of FDI. Workers in foreign firms learn the global frontier of productivity and how globalised production works. That knowledge sits with them, not with the company, and goes with them to other jobs and new firms. {111-C04}
~ “Again and again through world history,” he said, “we have seen that knowledge diffusion happening.”
stories.why: If knowledge moves a society forward, the foreign factory is, in Shah’s word, the crucible where it is made. What it teaches walks out of the gate with its workers, into new jobs and new firms.

quiz.q: What equity stake did the OECD and IMF agree makes an investment FDI?
quiz.a: Ten per cent: a 9 per cent stake counts as portfolio investment.

quiz.q: How many FDI numbers does the balance of payments produce, by Ajay Shah’s count?
quiz.a: Seven: gross flows, repatriations and nets for each direction, plus a ‘net net’.

quiz.q: Which foreign companies first set up garment businesses in Bangladesh, in Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: Taiwanese and South Korean companies; their local staff later started firms of their own.

quiz.q: Who coined the phrase “tariff-jumping FDI”, and when did he raise it?
quiz.a: Jagdish Bhagwati, in the early 1990s, when India’s first FDI surge arrived.

quiz.q: Why does India’s business community welcome portfolio investment but resist FDI, according to Shah?
quiz.a: FDI means competition; portfolio money means cheaper capital. Ila Patnaik figured it out.

quiz.q: In Indian software, which firms turned out less productive than pure exporters?
quiz.a: Those doing outbound FDI by body shopping staff into the UK and Germany.
